speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: asked the Minister for Health whether there can be a standby queue at COVID-19 vaccination centres to allow interested members of the public to take the place of those who do not turn up for their scheduled vaccination.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: asked the Minister for Health whether the Ministry will reconsider its stand and to allow Singaporeans who are required to travel for work and studies to opt in to receive early COVID-19 vaccination since more vaccine supplies have arrived.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: asked the Minister for Health whether there is a hotline number for members of the public who have had their COVID-19 vaccinations to call if they have queries regarding post-vaccination symptoms and for clarifications and assurance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: asked the Minister for Health whether staff and volunteers working in mosques can be prioritised for COVID-19 vaccination in preparation for conducting terawih and qiyamullail during the holy month of Ramadan.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Health whether volunteers and staff at congregational and worship services can be considered as frontline staff and prioritised for COVID-19 vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue our efforts to encourage the take-up of the vaccine.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our supply of vaccines remains limited by the ability of vaccine manufacturers to deliver, given the high levels of global demand.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This has resulted in limited booking slots in recent days.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I apologise for the inconvenience caused to those who have not been able to book earlier.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As more supplies arrive, we will progressively open more slots.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have had to prioritise our vaccinations, starting with our healthcare workers, vulnerable elderly and those involved in COVID-19 operations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Expert Committee on COVID-19 Vaccination had also recommended that we prioritise those personnel whose job roles are of critical importance to the functioning of Singapore and are at higher risk of exposure to and onward transmission of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is critical to ensure that key sectors would be able to continue functioning effectively even during a local outbreak, and further reduce risks to our vulnerable populations and the community at large.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Such personnel include those involved in safeguarding our borders and maintaining law and order, those involved in the provision of utilities such as water, energy and telecommunications services, workers who ensure the supply of essential food items, and land transport workers involved in ensuring that our transport services are kept running.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Religious workers might also face potential risks as they may engage in regular and non-transient contact with worshipers and devotees, including the elderly and vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Older religious workers, aged 45 and above, are already eligible for vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Religious workers are also required to comply with safe management measures in the conduct of religious services and in other engagements with worshippers or devotees.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We continue to make steady progress with our vaccination programme.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To date, about 60% of eligible seniors aged 70 and above, and close to 70% of eligible seniors aged 60 to 69 have received the COVID-19 vaccination or booked their vaccination appointments.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have recently invited citizens and residents aged 45 to 59 to begin to register for their vaccinations and close to 500,000, or about half, had done so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Those who have registered will progressively receive invitations through SMS to make appointments for their vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This may take some time given the number of people who have registered.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: People under the age of 45 have also been patiently waiting for their turn.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Based on current schedule, we plan to begin inviting them in June to book their slots.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If all goes well, we will complete the vaccination programme as scheduled by the end of the year.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some members of the public may wish to receive their vaccination early for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Since 16 March, we have opened up an appeals channel for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents who need to travel overseas on compassionate grounds, for employment or study purposes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They will need to submit sufficient documentation to support their appeal.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will prioritise appeals with earlier travel dates if they are able to complete the two-dose regimen prior to departure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Close to 98% of those who booked appointments for COVID-19 vaccinations in the last 30 days have showed up for their appointments.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We estimate that about 1% of those who turned up were rejected because of concerns about allergies and contra-indications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We encourage everyone to be vaccinated when your turn comes and to turn up at the vaccination appointments that you have made so that you do not deny another person the opportunity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, such cases do not result in vaccine wastage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We closely monitor the appointment bookings and historical take-up rate, and deliver the appropriate number of vaccine doses to the vaccination sites.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Unopened vials can be stored at the vaccination sites for at least three days.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Vaccination site providers will start a new vial only when they have checked that there are individuals awaiting vaccination, to avoid vaccine wastage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the end of the day, to utilise any balance remaining in a multi-dose vial and further minimise wastage, there are pre-planned lists of individuals who will be invited to be vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These could be staff who are working at the vaccination sites or frontline volunteers who have an active role in engaging seniors on vaccinations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As with other established vaccines, people who receive the COVID-19 vaccine may experience common side effects, such as pain at the injection site and fatigue.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Should the side effects persist or get worse after a few days, they should see a doctor and seek medical attention.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In very rare cases, the COVID-19 vaccine can cause a severe allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of face, throat, eyes or lips, a fast heartbeat, dizziness and weakness or a bad rash all over the body.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the event of a severe allergic reaction, please call 995 or visit the nearest hospital immediately.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Members of the public can also visit www.vaccine.gov.sg or the MOH website to further understand the post-vaccination symptoms.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will share more details about the studies once they are completed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Vaccination is a key enabler to reduce the risk of community transmission and allow more economic and community activities to resume.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The first is, the Senior Minister of State did explain about the measures taken to minimise wastage but I would nevertheless like to ask whether a standby system can be arranged to allow those who are not yet eligible for vaccination but willing to wait on standby basis at vaccination centres, to take the place of those who did not turn up, assuming the frontline people and volunteers have already had their turn.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, whether a standby system can be arranged for those who are willing, as it will take to the end of the year for the rest of the population to get their jab.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The second question relates to prioritising vaccination candidates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The point she makes about the prioritisation for workers in certain religious settings highlights the need for continued safe management measures and vigilance from everybody involved.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if there are specific individuals who might have particularly high risks, we will look at their situation and try our best to accommodate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First of all, could he confirm that there has actually been a change in the advice given to certain groups of people who initially were considered to be ineligible or asked to defer their vaccinations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By that, I mean in the initial stages of the online screening, people were asked whether they had allergies and whether they suffered from certain conditions, but I think there is now new advice given that these people who were originally considered not eligible, actually can take the vaccination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like him to confirm that there has been an update or a change in those instructions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And in that light, first, has the online screening been modified so that we do not exclude people who can actually take the vaccination; and secondly, are we catching up on those who were deemed to have failed the online screening initially but now with further scientific evidence they are actually eligible to take the vaccination?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How are we catching up with those people?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is severe anaphylactic reactions that we are most concerned about.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And as an increasing number of people has been vaccinated, we have confidence over the situations in which someone previously thought to be ineligible might now go forward and have the vaccine.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, the online systems and our various guidance to people manning counters and hotlines has changed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The way in which we are catching up is that the citizens involved remain as part of our patients, the patients of the healthcare providers, the vaccine system will continue to track this process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Most people are able to go forward and complete the vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If there are individuals who have been deemed ineligible, I would reinforce that this is about deferring the appointment and the consultation to a time where they might subsequently become eligible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to pay close attention to this segment of the population.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that he mentioned that the Government does not intend to measure the antibody levels of persons as it stands now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, would there not be a need to guard against variants and, in particular, the effect of this vaccination against variants?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As I have mentioned, we are studying the matter of antibody levels.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think before we make a decision about how we would look at what is happening in the population, let us, first, do those studies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For most vaccinations previously, that has not been the approach to go with a population-wide antibody assay.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is also logistically very difficult and would place a burden on our population.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think there are two separate issues – the issue of virus variants is being closely studied by our experts as well as international experts; and the matter of if, when and whether we should be doing serology and antibody testing is also being studied.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, let us complete those studies before we make any decision on that basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Two quick questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the diversity of vaccines that will eventually be deployed, I am wondering if there has been any effort by the Government in persuading take-up based on specific types of vaccines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am thinking, in particular, certain of my elderly residents may have a preference, for instance, for the Sinovac versus mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Related to this, the second question is whether the Ministry will actually have a threshold target for coverage associated with herd immunity and, if so, what would the next phase of relaxation of control measures look like were we to attain that threshold.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The take-up rate is healthy across the vaccines that have been licensed and are being used in our various centres.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, it is a bit premature to talk about that at this point in time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The target is for as many of our eligible residents as possible to be vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is a little bit premature to be then talking about the relaxation measures for the next phase when we have not reached it.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I just want to check for the essential services workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It was after I had submitted my Parliamentary Question that the announcement came for those who want to be vaccinated under a certain age group.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: But for workers in the essential services group, how do we then ensure that they are all vaccinated for the second dose in the appropriate time?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The risk is because we tend to mix with migrant workers a lot and we also do a lot of engagements.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier, as far as I am concerned, the first group of essential workers are those who were working during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We could not wait to complete every single essential worker before we then started with the elderly, the vulnerable or other at-risk groups.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we have a parallel processing, if you like, that essential workers continue to be vaccinated although most of them have largely been done so, together with the roll-out to the elderly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, just as now, not all the elderly are vaccinated, we have started with the next group and we will, in parallel, open up to more and more segments of our population as our vaccine supplies come in.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we will continue to pay close attention to make sure that those who are vulnerable or who are at high risk or who perform these essential functions will get priority.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of them may be for studies and some of them may be for other purposes, like looking after nephews, to attend weddings.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For some reason, MOH has applied quite strict criteria to those who have made the appeals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am asking MOH whether they will consider being more flexible about allowing people to get their vaccination earlier before they travel overseas, as contrasted to extending the vaccination programme to residents of a different age when they can be actually quite neutral about taking their vaccination earlier or later.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, we have one group who wants it earlier versus another group who are actually very neutral about whether they get their vaccination earlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, could MOH be a bit more flexible to allow those who want to get their vaccination earlier to get it earlier?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Even though there may be some people who are a little bit agnostic about exactly when they get it and are willing to defer, the reality is that we are vaccinating people as quickly as possible, given the supplies that come in.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, if we were to prioritise one group, it will be at the expense of another who currently wish to be vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The slots are booked and the capacity is being used up and the vaccines are being used up.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we recognise that there are people who wish to be prioritised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are criteria and it is very helpful that documentation is submitted to support those criteria and we will work our way through these appeals to try to help as many people to be vaccinated as soon as possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But, ultimately, the limit is not our wish to force people who are perhaps a little bit hesitant at this point – we do encourage everybody to do it – the limit is actually the rate at which the supplies are coming in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A few elderly residents told me they felt pain in their legs and their knees the day after vaccination.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One even showed me a rash at the vaccination area.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, they worry and they wonder if it was caused by the vaccination or would it go away or they needed to seek treatment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, I would like to propose if MOH would consider having a hotline manned by a multilingual team who can speak the mother tongue and dialects.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are two points which are slightly separate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One is the importance of making sure that we make our materials, transactions and interactions available in multiple languages.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, we will pay quite a lot of attention to this, especially on the ground at the service counters at the vaccination centres.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The separate issue is residents who then experienced symptoms after having had a vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What the Member is describing is a situation where one has clinical symptoms a day after vaccination and was worried about whether these are problems where you need medical help.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would suggest that perhaps a MOH hotline manned by our non-clinical staff may not be the best first port of call for residents in such a situation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If they have clinical symptoms, if they have persistent pain, persistent fever, rash and, especially things like difficulty breathing, what they need is to seek clinical help and they should do so from the relevant hospital, polyclinic and clinical care providers that are close to them.
